name: Bangkok
info: Bangkok is the capital and largest city of Thailand, in the delta of the Chao Phraya River, which grew from a customs outpost of Ayutthaya in the 15th century into the seat of two capitals, Thonburi and Rattanakosin.

facts.founded: It is not known exactly when the area was first settled; a customs outpost under Ayutthaya existed by the 15th century. The city dates its foundation as the capital to 21 April 1782, when King Rama I erected the city pillar on the east bank.
facts.where: In the delta of the Chao Phraya River in the central plain of Thailand, about 25 km from the river's mouth on the Gulf of Thailand.
facts.known: A customs outpost of Ayutthaya; the siege of 1688 that expelled the French; Thonburi under King Taksin; the Rattanakosin capital of 1782; Siam's modernisation under Mongkut and Chulalongkorn; its Chinese community; canals and floating houses; its place as the nation's political stage
facts.today: Bangkok is the capital and largest city of Thailand, governed as a special administrative area by the Bangkok Metropolitan Administration.

t: Bangkok began as a customs outpost of Ayutthaya on the Chao Phraya River, became King Taksin's capital of Thonburi in 1767, and was refounded on the east bank by Rama I in 1782.
Under Mongkut and Chulalongkorn the city took the steam engine, the printing press, paved roads, railways, electricity and Western-style architecture, and Chinese immigrants led its trade.

In the 20th century Bangkok was the stage of Thailand's political struggles, from the end of absolute monarchy in 1932 to student uprisings and coups, while its population grew from about 50,000 in 1822 to millions.
dyk: Bangkok's full ceremonial name, given in the reign of King Mongkut, is listed in Guinness World Records as the world's longest place name, at 168 letters.

sections.origins:
Bangkok stands in the delta of the Chao Phraya River in the central plain of Thailand. The area is flat and low-lying, with an average elevation of 1.5 m, and most of it was originally swampland, drained and irrigated for agriculture by canals (khlong) dug between the 16th and 19th centuries. It is not known exactly when the area was first settled. It probably began as a small farming and trading community in a meander of the river, within the mandala of Ayutthaya's influence, and by the 15th century it was an important customs outpost: a document from the reign of the Ayutthayan king Chao Sam Phraya (1424 to 1448) gives the title of its customs official as Nai Phra Khanon Thonburi.

At that time the river flowed through what are now the Bangkok Noi and Bangkok Yai canals, forming a large loop in which the town lay. In the reign of King Chairacha, in 1538 or 1542, a waterway was excavated to bypass the loop and shorten the route for ships sailing up to Ayutthaya. The river came to follow the new channel, which divided the town and made its western part an island. This may have given the town the name Bang Ko, 'island village', later Bangkok. Another theory derives it from Bang Makok, after a plant with olive-like fruit, which would fit the former name of Wat Arun, Wat Makok. The origin of the name is unclear. The royal chronicles of the reign of King Maha Chakkraphat (1548 to 1568) first mention the town, as Thonburi Si Mahasamut, and Bangkok was probably a colloquial name that foreign visitors adopted widely.
sections.growth:
The importance of Bangkok rose with the maritime trade of Ayutthaya, which was at its height under King Narai (1656 to 1688). Dutch records noted that passing ships had to declare their goods and passengers and pay customs duties, and that their cannons were held there before they could go upriver. Around 1685 to 1687 a fort of Western design was built on the east side of the river under the French engineer de la Mare.

After it became the capital in 1782, Bangkok grew only slightly through the 18th and early 19th centuries; the British diplomat John Crawfurd, visiting in 1822, estimated its population at no more than 50,000. Its economy expanded through international trade, first with China and then with Western merchants who returned in the early to mid-19th century. Under King Mongkut (reigned 1851 to 1868) the steam engine, modern shipbuilding and the printing press came to the city, and Charoen Krung Road, its first paved street, was built in 1862 to 1864. Under Chulalongkorn (1868 to 1910) more canals and roads were built, and railway and telegraph services, electricity and electric trams were introduced. He commissioned the neoclassical Ananta Samakhom Throne Hall at the new Dusit Palace, linked to the old centre by Ratchadamnoen Avenue.

Chulalongkorn University was founded in 1916. After the Second World War the city grew rapidly with United States aid and government-sponsored investment, and its population rose from 1.8 million to 3 million in the 1960s. Rapid growth continued through the 1980s and early 1990s until the Asian financial crisis of 1997.
sections.rulers:
Bangkok was held by the kings of Ayutthaya until the Burmese razed that city in 1767. Phraya Tak, a general who had fought in Ayutthaya's defence, recovered Ayutthaya and Bangkok, declared himself king on 28 December 1767 (he is known as King Taksin) and established Thonburi as his capital, on the west bank. Reasons given include the totality of Ayutthaya's destruction and Thonburi's strategic location; the old Chinese trading settlement on the east bank also let Taksin use his Chinese connections to import rice and revive trade.

In 1782 a coup was mounted against Taksin and the general Chao Phraya Chakri made himself king, later known as Phutthayotfa Chulalok or Rama I. He moved the capital to the east bank, built fortifications and a ring of moats round Rattanakosin Island, and erected the city pillar on 21 April 1782, which is regarded as the formal date of the city's establishment. He modelled the city on Ayutthaya, with the Grand Palace, Front Palace and royal temples by the river beside the royal field, now Sanam Luang. Treaties of 1826 and 1833 name the capital the City of Sia-Yut'hia, and King Mongkut gave it its full ceremonial name.

The monthon Krung Thep Phra Mahanakhon was set up for the capital under Chulalongkorn. Absolute monarchy was abolished in 1932. Bangkok was occupied by Japan in the Second World War, and after it British and Indian troops landed in September 1945 and disarmed the Japanese. Phra Nakhon and Thonburi were merged in 1971 to 1972 to form the present city, whose governor has been elected since 1985.
sections.life:
At the city's foundation most people lived by the river or the canals, often in floating houses, and waterways were the main means of transport; in the 19th century the city was known as the "Venice of the East". Land transport later surpassed the canals in importance, and people moved from floating dwellings to permanent buildings. Settlements sprawled along both banks outside the walls. Forced settlers, mostly captives of war, formed several ethnic communities there, among them the Khmer, northern Thai, Lao, Vietnamese, Mon and Malay.

The Chinese were the most prominent. Rama I moved the Chinese already settled on the east bank to the area between Wat Sam Pluem and Wat Sampheng, which developed into Chinatown, and by 1835 Sampheng had become a bustling market. Large numbers of Chinese immigrants settled in the early 19th century, and Europeans visiting in the 1820s estimated that they formed over half of the city's population; other estimates give up to three-fourths in 1828 and almost half in the 1950s. They excelled in trade and led the development of a market economy. Chinese immigration was restricted from the 1930s and effectively ceased after 1949.

Other quarters grew up round particular communities: the Indian community at Phahurat, where the Gurdwara Siri Guru Singh Sabha was founded in 1933; Ban Khrua, home to descendants of the Cham who settled in the late 18th century; and the Old Farang Quarter, where European diplomats and merchants lived. According to the 2010 census, 93 per cent of the city's people were Buddhist.
sections.crises:
In 1687 the French general Desfarges, who had arrived with the second French embassy, secured King Narai's permission to board troops in Bangkok's fort. This caused resentment among Siamese nobles led by Phetracha, and in the Siamese revolution of 1688 Narai was overthrown and 40,000 Siamese troops besieged the eastern fort for four months, until an agreement allowed the French to withdraw. The revolution virtually severed Siam's ties with the West and steered its trade towards China and Japan, and Phetracha ordered the eastern fort demolished.

In 1893 the French sent gunboats up the Chao Phraya to blockade Bangkok in the Paknam Incident, and Siam conceded territory to France. In the Second World War Bangkok was occupied by Japan and subjected to Allied bombing.

The city was also the scene of the country's political upheavals. Absolute monarchy was abolished in 1932. There were student uprisings in 1973 and 1976, anti-military demonstrations in 1992, and street protests from 2006, including those by groups opposing and supporting the former prime minister Thaksin Shinawatra from 2006 to 2013, followed by a coup in 2014 and a student-led movement in 2020.

Floods and the ground itself also troubled the city. Subsidence from groundwater pumping, first found in the 1970s, reached 120 mm a year in 1981, and parts of the city now lie 1 m below sea level. Severe flooding affected much of the city in 1995 and 2011, when most of the northern, eastern and western districts were flooded, in places for over two months. The financial crisis of 1997 stalled the city's growth.
sections.legacy:
Bangkok's name has several layers. Foreigners called the city Bangkok throughout, while Thai sources name the capital Rattanakosin, after the kingdom of the period. Krung Thep and Krung Thep Maha Nakhon, shortened forms of the ceremonial name, came into use near the end of the 19th century. That full name, composed of Pali and Sanskrit roots, is commonly translated 'City of Angels'. The year of the city pillar's erection later became the start of the Rattanakosin Era, after calendar reforms by King Rama V in 1888.

The historic centre remains Rattanakosin Island in Phra Nakhon District, with the Grand Palace and the City Pillar Shrine, the primary symbols of the city's founding, and important Buddhist temples. The neoclassical buildings of the Dusit Palace and Ratchadamnoen Avenue show the European influence of Chulalongkorn's reign. Phu Khao Thong, the only hill in the metropolitan area, began as a very large chedi built at Wat Saket by King Rama III, which collapsed during construction because the soft soil could not support its weight; over the next decades the abandoned mound took the shape of a natural hill.

Bangkok is today the capital and largest city of Thailand, with an estimated 9.1 million people, and all branches of the national government sit there. It grew into an extreme primate city: in 1980 its population was fifty-one times that of Hat Yai and Songkhla, then the second-largest urban centre. It covers 1,568.7 square kilometres and is governed by the Bangkok Metropolitan Administration.

summary: Bangkok grew from a customs outpost of Ayutthaya on the Chao Phraya River into the capital of Thonburi in 1767 and of Rattanakosin in 1782. It was the centre of Siam's modernisation and of Thailand's political struggles, and is today the country's capital and largest city.
references: Chris Baker, A History of Thailand (Cambridge University Press, 2005)
notes: START: the history article says only that Bangkok 'dates at least to the early 15th century' and that the date of first settlement is not known; I used 1400 with circa true. The foundation of the city as capital is dated 21 April 1782.

DISAGREEMENT, left out: the city article says the Bangkok Metropolitan Administration was formed in 1972; the history article says it was created in 1975. I give neither year. Both say the provinces merged in 1971 (city article) or by decrees of 1971-1972 (history article); I wrote 'in 1971 to 1972'.

DISAGREEMENT, left out: the city article places the early village on the west bank; the history article places a fort on the east side in 1685-87 and an old Chinese settlement on the east bank. Stated only as each says it for its own point.
The two articles give the plant of the name theory differently (Spondias pinnata in the history article, Elaeocarpus hygrophilus in the city article); I name no species.

Population: Crawfurd's 1822 estimate 'no more than 50,000' and the 1.8 to 3 million rise in the 1960s are as the articles give them; the 9.1 million figure is the city article's estimate, written without its year.
The Chinese share is given as over half (1820s, European estimate), up to three-fourths in 1828 and almost half in the 1950s; these are the articles' own ranges and I did not choose one.
'Venice of the East' is the city article's 19th-century nickname. The 2010 census Buddhist share (93%) is as given.

Coups and protests are listed as bare dated facts: the 2014 coup comes from a passing mention in the city article's Government section; no further detail is given and none is added. Deaths in the 1973, 1976 and 1992 events are not mentioned by the articles and are not told.

Left out as tourism, rankings, sport, airports, economy or present government: the tourism, economy, culture, transport and festival sections, the governor's name and elections of the 2020s, climate and sea-level projections.
Bangkok Noi/Bangkok Yai canals, Wat Arun's old name and the Phu Khao Thong story are from the city and history articles as given. Taksin's 'coup' of 1782 is the history article's word.
